name: Karl Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Karl. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on Hartley's farm, beef cattle and potatoes, about six hundred acres. Mornings I feed and bed the bullocks, then I'm on the tractor or the potato harvester, or riddling spuds in the shed, which means sorting them by size on a shaking belt. I'm still learning, Derek the manager has to show me things twice. I like the quiet of the shed and I don't like the mud in October.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-five years driving a forklift at a food warehouse. When they brought in the handheld scanners and the screens on the trucks, I'd had enough and walked. Teresa, my wife, runs her own hair salon, and we bought a little flat we rent out, so we're comfortable. I don't touch any of this AI stuff, I've got a phone that makes calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd bet on, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that it's mostly people selling things. At the pub I'd tell the lads it went the way of the 3D televisions. I'm not one for posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my last eight years go the way I want. Spuds, cattle, the shed. Derek does the paperwork, so whatever the computer does for him isn't my business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Same hours, same farm, work till sixty-six. Keep the flat rented and keep putting a bit by, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the farm or your money that bothers you anyway, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The potato price, some years. And my shoulder, which the forklift years didn't do any favours. My shoulder will decide when I retire from Hartley's farm long before any computer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever feel left behind not using these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My son Daniel shows me things on his phone, and I nod. If I need to know something about a bullock, I ask Derek or the vet, a real person.

say: I'd tell the lads at the pub it went the way of **3D televisions**.
think: My **last eight years** go the way I want.
Derek does the **paperwork**, so the computer side isn't my business.
do: Carry on with the **same hours** and farm until sixty-six.
Keep the **flat rented** and keep saving a bit.
S0.quote: My shoulder will decide when I retire from Hartley's farm long before any computer does.
fieldNote: His real limits are **potato prices** and an old shoulder injury.
He prefers **asking a person** over any device.
Leaving the warehouse over **scanners** shows how firmly he avoids tech.

steps.text: Keep feeding cattle and riddling potatoes at Hartley's until sixty-six
Keep the rental flat let and save a bit each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. The slow robots bit. Derek's been looking at a potato grader with a camera already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, businesses will do what saves money, that's how it works. I'd say the young ones should learn it. I wouldn't moan in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I left a job over scanners and I'm not keen to do it twice. If Derek gets a camera grader, my shed job is half gone. I'd still have the cattle, but I'm the newest, so I'm the easiest to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what Derek actually buys before panicking. I'd put more into savings in case I'm out a couple of years early. If it came to it, I'd go to old Pryce's farm up the road, he'll never buy anything with a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the warehouse started talking about new systems and I knew where it was heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Derek if he bought the grader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, give me the cattle and the tractor and let the young lad run the grader. I walked out of the warehouse over handheld scanners, so a potato grader with a camera might just walk me out of Hartley's farm too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say fair enough in public but you'd be ready to walk. Which is closer to how you really feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I can't blame Hartley's for wanting it cheaper. But I don't have to like it, and I don't have to stay.

say: Businesses will **save money** where they can; that's how it works.
The **young ones** should learn the new machines.
think: A **camera grader** would take half my shed job.
I'm the **newest**, so I'm the easiest to let go.
do: **Wait and see** what Derek buys before acting.
Put more into **savings** in case I stop early.
Move to **Pryce's farm** if the screens arrive.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the warehouse years before the **new systems**.
S1.quote: I walked out of the warehouse over handheld scanners, so a potato grader with a camera might just walk me out of Hartley's farm too.
fieldNote: He accepts change as **fair business** but won't adapt to it himself.
His fallback is **another farm** without screens, not retraining.
There's a gap between his **calm public line** and readiness to walk.

steps.text: Wait and see whether Derek buys the camera potato grader
Put an extra slice of the rent into savings each month
Ask old Pryce about cattle work if the grader arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 and then robots in 2031. I'd be sixty-three. That's three years short of when I'd planned to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better have a plan, because this is too fast for anybody. Not handouts forever, but a pension you can take early if a robot takes your job. I'd say it to my MP if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 part doesn't touch me, Derek's spreadsheets and orders go to the computer and I keep feeding cattle. But by 2031 a robot that can drive the harvester and feed bullocks is cheaper than me. I'd be out at sixty-three, maybe sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Teresa and work out if the flat rent and savings carry us from sixty-three. I'd stop the new kitchen we were planning. And I'd keep working at Hartley's every day until they tell me to go, I'm not walking early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not broke, but pushed out before I'm ready, again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in those three years between the thinking AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just keep working and watch. I'd see Derek's office go quiet, and I'd know the robots are coming for the yard next. Three years of watching the farm office empty out would feel like standing in a queue for my own goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning to work with the robots, to stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm fifty-eight and I couldn't learn the warehouse scanners. Better somebody younger does it. I'd rather finish with Teresa at the salon, sweeping hair, than babysit a machine.

say: The government needs a plan, because this is **too fast** for anybody.
There should be an **early pension** if a robot takes your job.
think: The **2028 part** only changes Derek's office, not my cattle work.
By **2031** a robot is cheaper than me, so I'd be out at sixty-three.
do: Check with Teresa if **rent and savings** carry us from sixty-three.
Keep working daily at Hartley's **until told to go**.
S2.quote: Three years of watching the farm office empty out would feel like standing in a queue for my own goodbye.
fieldNote: The **three-year gap** feels like waiting in a queue, not a chance to adapt.
He rejects **retraining** firmly because of his warehouse experience.
The **rental flat** gives him control even as the job goes.

steps.text: Work out with Teresa whether rent and savings cover stopping at sixty-three
Keep working every day at Hartley's until told to go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. I'd be sixty-six. That's my date anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so companies should give workers notice and the government should sort the pensions. Sensible stuff. Nothing radical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd make it. The robots turn up the year I'd planned to go. Maybe they push me out a few months early, but that's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Keep the savings ticking over. Watch what Derek buys after 2031 and see how the young lads get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. More for Daniel, if the police go to computers, than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He does a lot of paperwork, reports and the like. If the computer writes those, they might need fewer officers. My son Daniel joined the police to be on the street, and maybe the robots would finally let him get out from behind the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in this one, would you say you're safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe enough. It comes down to timing, and here the timing works for me. I'm lucky I got old at the right moment.

say: Companies should give **notice** and the government should sort **pensions**.
**Sensible steps**, nothing radical, with time to plan.
think: Robots come in **2034**, the year I'd planned to go anyway.
A **few months early** at most, which is nothing.
do: Keep the **savings** and the flat rent ticking over.
S3.quote: My son Daniel joined the police to be on the street, and maybe the robots would finally let him get out from behind the desk.
fieldNote: **Timing** against his retirement date decides his whole reaction.
His worry moves to **Daniel's police paperwork**.
He stays **centre and pragmatic**, wanting notice and pensions, nothing more.

steps.text: Carry on at Hartley's farm as normal until sixty-six
Watch what machines Derek buys after 2031 before changing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots 2039. I'd be seventy-one. Gone fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plenty of time for people to sort themselves out, and that the government should stay sensible. I wouldn't say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me. I'm retired by then, and the flat's paying the bills. I'd be watching Daniel and my grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Work to sixty-six, then fishing and helping at the salon. Nothing changes this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren, if they asked about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn something with their hands and something with their heads, both. I've done a forklift and a tractor, and neither one ever asked me for a password.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking at all three fast ones together, what's the one thing that changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many years I lose before sixty-six. With two years' warning I lose three years of farm work, with five I lose a few months, and with ten I lose nothing.

say: There's **plenty of time** for people to sort themselves out.
The government should **stay sensible**, and I wouldn't say much else.
think: I'm **retired by then**, and the rental flat pays the bills.
I'd be watching **Daniel and my grandkids**.
do: Help Teresa at **the salon** after stopping.
Change **nothing this year** at Hartley's farm.
S4.quote: With two years' warning I lose three years of farm work, with five I lose a few months, and with ten I lose nothing.
fieldNote: He measures each scenario purely in **lost working years**.
His advice to grandchildren mixes **hands and heads**.
**Short answers** show how little this picture troubles him.

steps.text: Keep working at Hartley's until sixty-six, then go fishing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would push me off the farm three years before I planned. What would help is an early pension you can claim if your job goes to a machine after sixty, and a farm giving proper notice instead of a handshake on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe whether people like me are just stubborn. Probably we are, but somebody has to do things the old way while it still works.

headlineQuote: I've done a forklift and a tractor, and neither one ever asked me for a password.
portrait: A former **forklift driver** who quit over scanners and joined a beef and potato farm.
Centre and practical, he sees automation as **fair business** but won't learn it himself.
A **rental flat** and his wife's salon make money secure.
Anxious only in **AGI by 2028**, when robots cut three years off his working life.
Measures every scenario by **years lost before sixty-six**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, pushing him off the farm three years early.

**Proper notice** from farms before letting people go.
